question: What is the main job of the body's immune system when it comes to body tissues?

options.A: To destroy the body's own healthy cells
options.B: To distinguish between self and non-self
options.C: To produce energy for cellular repair
options.D: To circulate red blood cells through tissue

explanation: Spot on! The immune system's core superpower is knowing the difference between what belongs to your body (self) and foreign invaders (non-self). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h1)

question: What happens if the immune system gets confused and fails to recognize the body's own tissues?

options.A: Blood pressure drops to dangerously low levels
options.C: Red blood cells stop carrying oxygen
options.D: The body becomes completely immune to all viruses

explanation: You've got it! When the immune system stops recognizing 'self,' it mistakenly attacks healthy tissues, leading to autoimmune conditions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h1)

question: Which type of immunity are we born with as our body's built-in, general defense?
explanation: Nice work! Innate immunity is your natural, everyday shield that you are born with—like your skin and mucous membranes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h2)

question: Why does adaptive immunity fight off a familiar germ much faster and stronger the second time around?

options.A: Because innate barriers disappear over time
options.B: Because the germ becomes weaker inside the body
options.D: Because white blood cells multiply without stopping

explanation: Spot on! Your adaptive immune system keeps memory cells from past infections so it can launch a fast, targeted attack if the germ returns. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h2)

question: What is the biggest perk of active immunity compared to passive immunity?

options.A: It requires no cellular activity from the body
options.B: It provides long-lasting protection through memory cells
options.C: It works instantly within a few seconds
options.D: It can be transferred easily through touch

explanation: Well done! Active immunity gets your own cells to build long-term memory, keeping you protected for years. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h3)

question: A patient is rushed to the clinic after a snakebite and receives ready-made antibodies. What type of immunity is this?
explanation: Correct! Giving ready-made antibodies is passive immunity because the patient didn't have to manufacture them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h3)

question: How does a newborn baby naturally receive passive immunity from their mother?

options.A: Through breast milk and across the placenta
options.B: By developing mild infections in the nursery
options.C: By receiving routine infant vaccinations at birth
options.D: Through exposure to sunlight during infancy

explanation: You nailed it! Mums pass helpful antibodies to their babies across the placenta during pregnancy and through breast milk after birth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h4)

question: Which of these is a clear example of artificial active immunity?

options.A: Getting a polio vaccine at the primary health clinic
options.B: Drinking colostrum from a mother immediately after birth
options.C: Catching chickenpox from a classmate at school
options.D: Receiving snake antivenom after a bite on the farm

explanation: Spot on! Vaccines introduce harmless germ parts (antigens) so your body actively builds its own defense. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h4)

question: In immunology, what exactly is an antigen?

options.A: A medication used to lower systemic inflammation
options.B: A foreign substance that triggers an immune response
options.C: A physical barrier found in human skin layers
options.D: A white blood cell that produces Y-shaped proteins

explanation: Great job! An antigen is any foreign molecule that sounds the alarm and gets your immune cells ready for battle. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h5)

question: Once antibodies are released into the bloodstream, what is their primary mission?

options.A: To lock onto specific antigens and neutralize them
options.B: To break down food molecules in the stomach
options.C: To carry oxygen from the lungs to body tissues
options.D: To form hard physical barriers around open wounds

explanation: Correct! Antibodies act like custom-built locks that attach to matching antigens to neutralize them or mark them for destruction. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h5)

question: Who benefits the most when a community achieves herd immunity?

options.B: Only individuals with strong innate immunity
options.C: Vulnerable people who cannot receive vaccines
options.D: Only adults who travel to other countries

explanation: Spot on! Herd immunity builds a protective ring around fragile individuals who cannot take vaccines themselves. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h6)

question: What tends to happen when vaccination rates drop too low in a neighborhood or community?

options.A: Innate barriers become stronger to compensate
options.B: Antibody levels in newborn babies increase
options.C: Natural immunity replaces the need for shots

explanation: You got it! When herd immunity dips, preventable diseases find open doors to cause new outbreaks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h6)

question: Which of these options does NOT weaken or suppress a person's immune system?

options.A: Chronic high levels of physical and mental stress
options.B: Adequate daily nutrition and balanced diet

explanation: Nice work! Good food and a balanced diet nourish and support your immunity rather than harming it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h7)

question: Why is an elderly patient with poorly controlled diabetes at a much higher risk for a slow-healing foot infection?

options.A: Too much active immunity from childhood vaccines
options.B: Impaired white blood cell and immune function
options.C: An excess of maternal antibodies in the blood
options.D: Overactive innate barriers on the skin surface

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like diabetes and aging can slow down white blood cell activity, making it harder to fight off infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h7)
